title: Game: Set Match
bodyHtml:
Consider the word walruses and the phrase cheerful walruses. The diagram below shows one way to illustrate the relationship between these phrases.

Each circle stands for the set of things that could be described by the relevant word or phrase. Since all cheerful walruses are walruses, the region for cheerful walruses is fully contained inside the region for walruses. The sizes of the circles are irrelevant; what matters is how they overlap and which ones are contained inside others.

This example relates to an important question: how does the meaning of a phrase relate to the meanings of the words that make it up? This question comes up in computational linguistics because computers that process language must be able to determine the meanings of complex phrases.

Note that this problem only gives a partial picture of meaning in language. Some nuances that are left out are important in linguistic theories, but for the sake of this problem you should only use the information presented.

Below are 18 words and phrases in arbitrary order, along with a diagram representing their meanings.

LabelPhraseLabelPhraseLabelPhrase
Aalleged spiesGfruitsMpurple Italian cars
BberriesHfuture spiesNsmall big elephants
Cbig elephantsIgreen carsOsmall blueberries
DblueberriesJgreen Italian carsPsmall elephants
EcarsKhappy spiesQspies
FelephantsLItalian carsRstrawberries

Notes. Alleged spies are people who have been accused of being spies but who may or may not actually be spies. The phrase small big elephants may be confusing without context; here is an example where it can occur: “That’s a big elephant, but compared to other big elephants it’s relatively small; it’s a small big elephant.” We assume that cars cannot be both green and purple at the same time. We use the informal definition of berry, in which strawberries are a type of berry. We assume that elephants cannot be spies.

assets.alt: A large circle labelled walruses, containing a smaller circle labelled cheerful walruses.
Four groups of overlapping and nested circles, with regions numbered 1 to 18.

questions.partPrompt: Each of the words or phrases A–R corresponds to one of the regions 1–18 in the diagram. Enter the letter for each region.

hints.text: Work group by group. Each of the four diagram groups covers one topic: fruit, cars, spies, elephants. Decide which group is which before you place any individual region.

Adjectives do not all behave the same way. Some narrow a set from the inside — every green car is a car, so green cars sits inside cars. Others do not: an alleged spy might not be a spy at all, and a future spy is not a spy yet. Those adjectives produce circles that only overlap, or sit entirely outside.

Worked example: the spies group. Region 12 is the plain set, spies. Happy spies (14) are genuinely spies, so that circle sits inside 12. Alleged spies (11) only overlap 12, because some alleged spies are real and some are not. Future spies (13) sit entirely outside 12 — they are not spies yet. Now apply the same three shapes to the elephant group, where big and small are the interesting cases.

explanationHtml:
The problem is really asking you to sort adjectives into three classes by what they do to a set.

Intersective adjectives

These narrow a set from the inside. Every green car is a car, so green cars is a circle wholly inside cars. Fruits and berries work the same way: strawberries and blueberries sit inside berries, which sits inside fruits. That gives the nesting of group one: 1 fruits, 2 berries, 3 strawberries, 4 blueberries, 5 small blueberries.

Non-subsective adjectives

These break the containment entirely. An alleged spy may or may not be a spy, so the circle overlaps spies without being contained by it — region 11. A future spy is not a spy at all right now, so region 13 sits outside 12 altogether, touching only the alleged circle.

Subsective but relative adjectives

This is the elephant group, and the sharpest part of the problem. Big and small are subsective: every big elephant is an elephant. But they are judged relative to a comparison class, which is why small big elephants is not a contradiction. Region 18 sits inside region 17 (big elephants), not inside region 16 (small elephants) — a small big elephant is still a big elephant.

The cars group

The one place two circles overlap without either containing the other is 7 and 10, green cars and Italian cars. Their intersection is 8, green Italian cars. Since a car cannot be both green and purple, purple Italian cars (9) sits inside Italian cars but never touches the green circle.

Why this matters for computational linguistics: a system that assumes every adjective narrows its noun will conclude that an alleged spy is a spy. Knowing which class an adjective belongs to is what stops that.
